findings.evidence: livedo reticularis on the right arm (caption); violaceous broken reticular mottling visible on the arm

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real human patient explicitly described in the caption as having Sneddon syndrome, showing livedo reticularis on the right arm (with additional sites noted). The article title and in-text mentions confirm Sneddon syndrome and written informed consent for this patient. The visible violaceous net-like mottling is the classic cutaneous manifestation of Sneddon syndrome, mapped to the vocabulary finding sneddon_syndrome_livedo_racemosa (livedo reticularis is a listed synonym). No subtype is specified in the caption or vocabulary, so subtype is null. The group median age is not patient-specific, so age_group is unknown. Skin is adequately lit and appears light; no ethnicity is stated and no annotations are present.

in_text_mentions: The Medical Research Ethics Committee of the University Medical Centre Utrecht, The Netherlands, provided a waiver for this study. Informed consent was waived, as this is a retrospective study using anonymized patient data. We did obtain written informed consent from the patient of whom we showed the livedo reticularis in Fig 1.

We included 34 patients in the SS group, 14 patients in the isolated LR group and 41 patients in the control group. Eighty-eight percent of the patients in the SS group were female with a median age at diagnosis of 40.5 years. The median age at skin biopsy ranged from 42.0 to 52.0 years in all groups (Table 1). LR was most commonly present on the arms, legs and trunk (Fig 1). The median number of locations with livedo was 3 in the SS group and 2 in the isolated LR group.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real human skin-biopsy H&E from the Sneddon-syndrome skin-biopsy study; the boxed deep-dermal artery corresponds to the non-inflammatory cutaneous arteriolopathy ('probable occlusive microangiopathy') named in the caption. Disease attribution rests on the disease-focused article title plus this specific captioned manifestation, so confidence is moderate given the same pattern was also reported in isolated livedo and control biopsies. B: High-power H&E of the same biopsy showing thickened dermal arteriolar walls with patent lumens and neovascularization, directly matching the vocabulary finding sneddon_syndrome_cutaneous_obliterative_arteriolopathy (arteriolar wall thickening/intimal hyperplasia). Disease-focused article title plus the specific captioned manifestation support attribution to Sneddon syndrome; the term 'neovascularization' is explicitly in the caption but absent from the vocabulary, so it is listed as a proposed finding.

A: Digital subtraction angiography (late arterial phase) of the right ICA AP view in a patient discharged with a diagnosis of Sneddon syndrome (article title and in-text confirm SS). Shows multifocal distal branch narrowing, parietal irregularities and watershed blush — the most common angiographic abnormality of SS per the in-text ('stenosis and/or occlusion of intracranial vessels'). Real patient image, directly attributable to SS. B: Digital subtraction angiography (late arterial phase) of the right ICA lateral view in the same Sneddon syndrome case. Arrows indicate multifocal distal cortical branch narrowing and parietal irregularities, matching the in-text description of segmental intracranial arteriopathy ('stenosis and/or occlusion of intracranial vessels'), the most common angiographic finding in SS. Real patient image, disease attribution explicit. C: Digital subtraction angiography (late arterial phase) of the left ICA AP view...

[A] Right internal carotid artery (ICA) on anteroposterior (AP) view. [B] Right ICA on lateral view. [C] Left ICA on AP view. [D] Left ICA on lateral view.
in_text_mentions: Cerebral angiography (Figure 2) revealed slowed distal blood flow of cerebral arteries with decreased vessel diameter and parietal irregularities suggestive of vasculitis. The venous phase was normal, and there was no vascular malformation. The anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries in their respective distal segments showed segmental lesions with reduced caliber associated with tortuosity and slowed flow, characterizing a late blush in the territory of the watershed zone. The patient was discharged from the hospital with a diagnosis of SS and the following treatment: acetylsalicylic

The finding of vasculitis on cerebral angiography was the last piece in the puzzle of this case. Had this been the sole finding, it would have posed a major diagnostic challenge. Cerebral angiography is abnormal in up to 75% of patients with SS. The most common abnormality is an obliterating non-inflammatory arteriopathy, with stenosis and/or occlusion of intracranial vessels (Figure 2). In our case, cerebral DSA revealed decreases in calibration, contour irregularities, and blockages mainly in anterior circulation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial FLAIR MRI of a human patient with Sneddon syndrome showing a cortical/subcortical hyperintense lesion consistent with chronic ischemic injury; article title and in-text confirm Sneddon syndrome diagnosis. B: Axial FLAIR MRI of a human patient with Sneddon syndrome showing multifocal cortical/subcortical hyperintensities consistent with chronic ischemic injury. C: Axial FLAIR MRI of the posterior fossa in a human patient with Sneddon syndrome showing a right cerebellar hemisphere hyperintense lesion compatible with a chronic ischemic infarct, consistent with the multifocal chronic ischemic process described. D: Axial FLAIR MRI of a human patient with Sneddon syndrome showing periventricular white matter hyperintensities consistent with chronic ischemic injury.

panels.figure_caption: Axial Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery — FLAIR-weighted MRI images demonstrating multiple hyperintense lesions involving both cortical and subcortical regions, predominantly affecting the frontal and parietal lobes, with associated deep and periventricular white matter involvement, consistent with chronic ischemic injury. In the posterior fossa, an axial FLAIR image reveals a hyperintense lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere, compatible with a chronic ischemic infarct. Overall, the imaging pattern suggests a multifocal, chronic ischemic process involving multiple vascular territories, affecting both supratentorial and infratentorial structures.
